Our Story

She had been lying there for three days.

That's the visit Felicia Stallworth, RN, still thinks about — the one that convinced her to stop trying to fix a broken system from the inside, and build a different one instead.

I arrived for what should have been a routine supervisory nursing assessment — a home care check-in to confirm that the aide services billed to Medicaid were actually being delivered. What I found was a woman in her late seventies, in her own bed, in her own home, who had not been bathed since the aide last showed up — three days prior.

I documented everything. I always did. The functional limitations. The missed services. The patient's condition. The dates. The signatures. The filed paperwork. I brought it to the agency. Their response: "The patient's needs were not communicated properly." I had communicated them. In writing. Signed. Dated. Filed.

"The documentation was perfect. The care was absent. That contradiction is the story of a broken system — and it is the reason I decided to build a different one."

For twenty-four years as a Registered Nurse in Suffolk County and on the East End of Long Island, I watched the same cycle repeat: agencies billing for services never rendered, patients left without bathing or medication reminders, and a nurse — me — blamed for a gap I had documented in writing every time.

I watched something else, too: a specific kind of silence in homes where a patient and their aide couldn't speak the same language. Spanish-speaking seniors who couldn't tell their English-only aide they were in pain, or scared, or falling. English-speaking patients paired with aides who couldn't understand them either. Not one program on the East End trained PCAs or HHAs bilingually — while Spanish-speaking workers across Suffolk County who wanted to become certified aides had nowhere to learn.

And even when a trained aide found a placement here, the housing math broke the pipeline. A certified aide earning $18–$22 an hour cannot sustain life in East Hampton, where a shared room runs $1,500–$2,000 a month. So aides commuted 60 to 90 minutes each way from Brentwood or Riverhead — until the car broke down, or the exhaustion won, and the patient was told their aide was "no longer available."

It wasn't a workforce motivation problem. It was a housing math problem. And housing math problems don't fix themselves.

So I decided to build the pipeline — training, placement, veteran housing, and aide housing, every link owned and accountable, so that every promise made in the intake paperwork is kept at the bedside.

"Every service I promise, I will deliver. Every aide I train carries my RN license behind their certificate. Every patient in my care will be seen, supported, and never left wondering when help is coming. I built this because I watched the alternative fail — for 24 years — and I could not watch it fail one more day."

— Felicia Stallworth, RN, Founder, Felicia's Care Network
Our Mission

Every promise kept in practice — in English, and in Spanish.

Felicia's Care Network exists to solve Long Island's home care workforce crisis through dignified training, ethical placement, and innovative housing solutions — ensuring that every patient receives the care they were promised, every trained aide has a place to live and a career to build.

Our Vision

A Long Island where no one waits for care that never comes.

A Long Island where no senior goes without care because there is no one trained to provide it. Where no Spanish-speaking patient is isolated by a language barrier. Where no trained aide leaves the East End because they cannot afford to stay. And where no nurse ever has to fear losing their license for documenting the truth.

What we stand for

Core Values

Six operational commitments that govern every training session, every placement, every housing unit, and every patient interaction.

01 Integrity

We document what we do and we do what we document. There is no gap between our care plan and our care delivery — and there never will be.

02 Dignity

Every patient, every aide, every veteran is a person — not a billing code, not a headcount, not a shift to fill.

03 Equity

Bilingual care is not a luxury. Every Spanish-speaking patient deserves an aide who speaks their language — and every Spanish-speaking worker deserves training in theirs.

04 Accountability

We do not pass blame. We accept responsibility, fix problems, and protect the people who report them — because accountability is what safety looks like in practice.

05 Excellence

Our training is RN-led because the standard of care should be set by the highest credential in the room, not the lowest.

06 Community

We house our aides because workforce stability is patient safety. Our network rises and falls together.

Professional Biography

Felicia Stallworth, RN

Felicia Stallworth is a Registered Nurse with over 24 years of clinical and home care nursing experience in Suffolk County, New York. Throughout her career, she has provided direct nursing care, developed comprehensive patient care plans, supervised personal care and home health aide teams, and served as a relentless patient advocate within Long Island's East End home care system.

She is the founder of Felicia's Care Network, a vertically integrated care ecosystem that includes a BPSS-licensed health career training school, a licensed home care staffing agency, a veteran care residence, and a GoFundMe-supported aide workforce housing initiative. As Nurse Instructor of Felicia's Health Career Training School, she personally oversees all PCA and HHA curriculum delivery, in both English and Spanish.

Felicia Stallworth is a licensed Registered Nurse in the State of New York, based in East Hampton, NY, and is available for speaking engagements, media interviews, and community partnerships related to home care workforce development, veteran care, and Long Island's caregiving crisis.

Felicia's Health Career Training School

The East End's only bilingual PCA & HHA certification program.

BPSS-approved, RN-led, and taught in English and Spanish — because language should never be a barrier to entering the caregiving workforce or receiving quality care.

See the Curriculum
Two credentials, one bilingual standard

Programs & Pricing

PCA Certification

Personal Care Aide — 40 Hours — $750

18 hours theory, 22 hours hands-on skills lab. Intensive (5–7 days) or part-time evening (2–3 weeks) formats. Materials provided in English and Spanish at no extra charge. Maximum 12 students per cohort. Awards a BPSS Certificate of Completion (New York State).

HHA Certification

Home Health Aide — 75 Hours — $1,400

45 hours theory, 30 hours supervised clinical practicum. Prepares graduates for LHCSA, CHHA, and LTHHCP employment; graduates are listed on the NY State Home Care Registry within 5 business days. Payment plans and WIOA funding available.

Cultural Competency

Woven through every session, not a standalone module

Felicia Stallworth's 24 years of home care practice on the East End inform how the program teaches aides to earn trust and deliver safe, dignified care across cultures — how patients express pain, cultural norms around accepting help, family-centered decision-making, and respectful forms of address (señora, don, doña).

"In 24 years of home care on the East End, I have watched Spanish-speaking patients suffer — not because there were no aides willing to help, but because the aides who showed up could not speak their language and did not understand their culture. That is a clinical failure, and it is preventable."

— Felicia Stallworth, RN, Director, Felicia's Health Career Training School

Felicia's Veteran Home  ·  East Hampton, NY

A real home for those who served — priced to fit Aid & Attendance.

Private-room housing for wartime veterans and surviving spouses, in a genuine neighborhood home rather than an institution — with all-inclusive pricing built around VA benefit levels.

Compare Your Options

Who this home is for

Veterans and surviving spouses on a fixed VA income

Primary residents are veterans aged 65–85, primarily from the Vietnam and Gulf War eras, typically receiving $1,478–$2,788/month in Aid & Attendance pension benefits plus Social Security — but facing a stark gap between what nursing homes and assisted living cost and what a fixed VA income can actually cover.

Surviving spouses of wartime veterans, often aged 70–90 and receiving the $1,478/month A&A surviving-spouse rate, frequently face loneliness, safety concerns living alone, and unfamiliarity with the survivor benefits available to them.

Felicia's Veteran Home exists to close that gap: a real neighborhood home with personalized attention, built-in community, and transparent, all-inclusive pricing.

Frequently asked questions

Aid & Attendance, answered plainly

Does Aid & Attendance pay for housing?

A&A is a cash benefit the veteran or surviving spouse can use for any qualifying care-related expense, including housing in a setting where care is provided or available.

Can a surviving spouse receive A&A?

Yes. Surviving spouses of qualifying wartime veterans who meet the medical and financial criteria may receive A&A at the surviving-spouse rate ($1,478/month in 2026).

How long does it take to receive benefits?

Processing times vary. A Veterans Service Organization (VSO) can help expedite the claim. Benefits are often paid retroactively to the date of application once approved.

Is A&A the same as Medicaid?

No. A&A is a VA pension benefit for wartime veterans; it is entirely separate from Medicaid and does not affect Medicaid eligibility in most states.

Does the veteran need to be service-connected disabled?

No. A&A is a pension benefit, not a service-connected disability compensation benefit — service-connected disability is not required to qualify.

Can a veteran move in while an A&A application is pending?

Yes. A veteran may move in while the A&A application is pending — benefits are typically paid retroactively to the date the claim was filed.

Rooms are available now.

Reach out to ask about availability, pricing, or how to apply your Aid & Attendance benefit toward a room at Felicia's Veteran Home.

The Aide Housing Initiative

House our aides. Heal our community.

Every donated dollar puts a trained caregiver in a home near the patient who needs them.

Donate Now See Donation Tiers
The problem

The housing math that breaks the pipeline

A trained aide earning $18–$22 an hour cannot afford a room on the East End of Long Island. A shared room in East Hampton runs $1,500–$2,000 a month; a studio, when one is available at all, can exceed $3,000. So the aide we trained — the bilingual aide who knows how to transfer a patient safely, who speaks Spanish to the grandmother in Montauk who hasn't been understood by a caregiver in years — commutes from Brentwood, from Riverhead, from Central Islip. Sixty, seventy, ninety minutes each way. Until it doesn't work anymore. And the patient is left without care again.

This campaign breaks that cycle.

What your donation funds

Specifically, exactly, this:

  • Furnished shared rooms at Felicia's East Hampton property — housing 2 to 4 aides at a time
  • Utilities, WiFi, and laundry — so a working aide never chooses between the lights and the bus fare
  • A clean, safe, stable home base while aides earn their footing on the East End
  • Transitional housing terms of 3 to 12 months — long enough to build local roots and stay in the community that needs them

This is not a shelter. It is a launching pad — the missing link in a care pipeline that is otherwise complete: training, certification, placement, and now, a place to sleep so a caregiver can show up for their patient in the morning.

Every amount makes a difference

Who benefits

Not an abstract donation — something specific, for someone real

  • The trained aide who finally has a place to rest after their shift
  • The 84-year-old veteran in Springs who gets his bath this morning because someone could afford to be there
  • The Spanish-speaking abuela in East Hampton whose aide speaks to her in her own language for the first time
  • The adult daughter in Connecticut who stops lying awake at night, knowing this time care actually showed up
  • The entire East End community, which is only as strong as its capacity to care for its most vulnerable members
“I trained the aides. I placed the aides. And I am asking you — my community, Long Island, anyone who has ever had a family member who needed someone to show up and didn't — to help me house them.”
Felicia Stallworth, RN — Founder & Director
